newsitem.title: USA: Reno authorizes death penalty in Unabomber case.
newsitem.headline: Reno authorizes death penalty in Unabomber case.

text.p: U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno has authorised prosecutors to seek the death penalty for Unabomber suspect Theodore Kaczynski, Justice Department sources and a lawyer for the Kaczynski family said on Thursday.
Washington, D.C., attorney Anthony Bisceglie said he had informed Kaczynski's brother David and his mother Wanda of Reno's decision allowing prosecutors to seek the death penalty in the case.

Kaczynski, a 54-year-old former mathematics professor, is accused of being the shadowy Unabomber, who killed three people and injured 23 during an anti-technology bombing campaign between 1978 and 1995.

Kaczynski has been charged in Sacramento, California, with four bomb attacks between 1985 and 1995 that killed timber industry lobbyist Gilbert Murray and computer store owner Hugh Scrutton and injured two prominent scientists.
Kaczynski, who was arrested in Montana in April last year, has pleaded not guilty to the Sacramento charges. His trial is due to start in November.
In a statement about Reno's decision, Bisceglie said, "The family is devastated by this development and they are in seclusion at this time.
"We believe that the attorney general's decision is a terrible mistake, but we remain hopeful that justice will ultimately prevail in this tragic case," he said.
Bisceglie said a request for a meeting with Reno had been denied last week.

But the lawyer and David Kaczynski met with a Justice Department committee in January, urging them not to seek the death penalty. The family members have said the writings of Kaczynski, who lived in seclusion in a Montana shack, showed he was deeply troubled mentally.

"There are people in this world (who) are mentally ill. Are we going to start killing them," Wanda Kaczynski said in an interview with CBS' "60 Minutes" last year. "What kind of barbaric society are we headed for."
The family also argued that only after they went to the FBI with their suspicions was the agency able to solve the case, after a long, unsuccessful hunt for the bomber.
David Kaczynski has said that seeking the death penalty in the case would discourage other family members from coming forward with their suspicions in future cases.

Justice Department sources confirmed Reno had authorised the death penalty, and said the decision was expected to be disclosed in a court filing later on Thursday in Sacramento. They said she followed the recommendations of prosecutors.
Bisceglie said he was notified of the decision by prosecutor Robert Cleary, who offered no explanation why the death penalty would be sought.
Although the charges against Kaczynski carry a possible death penalty, it had not been known until Thursday whether prosecutors would seek that punishment if he is convicted.
Kaczynski also has been indicted in New Jersey over a 1994 bombing that killed an advertising executive. That case has been put on hold while the Sacramento one goes forward.
